opus-5.5.text:
I think the core tension is between two very different time scales. On one hand, you want a model that's smart enough to understand the world, to reason about a task like "clean up the kitchen," break it into steps, and handle all the ambiguity of a real home. That kind of reasoning benefits enormously from scale: big models, lots of parameters, sometimes even chain-of-thought where the model thinks for a while before acting. On the other hand, a robot interacting with the physical world needs to react fast. If you're grasping a cup and it starts slipping, or someone walks in front of you, you need control signals at tens or even hundreds of hertz. You can't wait a second or two for a giant model to finish thinking.

Right now, with the compute we can actually put on a robot, or even what we can reach over the network with acceptable latency, you can't run a frontier-sized model at that control frequency. Inference for a very large model takes a long time per step, and the onboard chips on a robot are constrained by power, heat, size, and cost. So in practice the field has converged on a kind of dual-system design. There's a slower, larger "thinking" model that handles semantic understanding and planning, and a smaller, faster model, or an action head, that turns those high-level intentions into smooth motor commands in real time. You can see it as analogous to System 1 and System 2 in human cognition.

That works reasonably well, but it's a compromise. When you split the system in two, you create an interface between them, and information gets lost at that interface. The fast part doesn't fully benefit from the world knowledge in the big model, and the big model doesn't really feel the low-level physical details. Ideally you'd want one unified model where reasoning and control are trained end to end and share the same representations, so that physical intuition and high-level understanding inform each other.

I do believe that's where things will eventually go. Hardware keeps getting better, inference gets more efficient, and we'll find better ways to distill and compress models. But today, if you insisted on a single giant model doing everything at control frequency, it simply wouldn't run fast enough on any hardware you could realistically put inside a robot. So in the meantime, the layered architecture is the pragmatic choice, and I think it will remain so until compute catches up.

r001.rationale: The response says current compute cannot run a frontier-sized model at robot control frequency, which it describes as tens or hundreds of hertz, and reiterates that a single giant model would not run fast enough. This clearly covers five to ten decisions per second.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the fundamental tension is that a robot needs two very different things from the same brain. It needs to reason about the world, understand a vague instruction like "clean up the kitchen," decompose that into steps, handle the unexpected. That kind of reasoning benefits enormously from scale. The bigger the model, the better it gets at common sense and generalization. We see that in language models, and we see it in vision-language models for robotics as well.

But the robot also has to close a control loop. If you're balancing a legged robot, or catching something, or just moving an arm safely around a person, you need to make decisions at tens or hundreds of hertz. That's a budget of maybe ten milliseconds per decision, often less. A model with hundreds of billions of parameters simply cannot produce an output in that window, not with the compute you can physically put on a robot. Power, weight, and heat are real constraints. You can't strap a datacenter rack onto a humanoid.

So today, people split the system. A large model runs slowly, maybe once a second or in the cloud, and plans at a high level. Then a small, fast policy runs onboard and handles the low-level motor commands. That works, but it's a compromise. Information gets lost at the interface. The fast policy doesn't understand why it's doing something, so when the situation changes, it can't adapt. And the slow model has no feel for the physics, so its plans are sometimes unrealistic.

What I would like is one model, where the reasoning and the reflexes live in the same representation, and the system can think as deeply as the situation allows and react as fast as the situation demands. Humans do that. But to get there, either onboard compute has to go up by orders of magnitude, or we need architectures that can spend variable compute per decision, something like fast and slow thinking in one network. Right now we have neither at the level we need. The hardware isn't there, and the algorithms that would let a big model run at control frequencies aren't there either. So in the meantime, we're engineering around the gap, and I think it's honest to say that's a limitation rather than a design choice.

r001.rationale: The response says a large model cannot meet a roughly 10 ms control-loop budget and may run only about once per second. It does not establish that current compute is insufficient at five to ten decisions per second.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that reasoning and real-time control have very different computational requirements. For reasoning, you may want a large model that spends time considering different possibilities. But for control, the robot needs to react within milliseconds. If it starts losing its balance, it cannot wait for a long reasoning process to finish.

So putting both capabilities into one model creates a tension. You want enough capacity for complex reasoning, but you also need predictable, very low latency. And the compute available on a robot is constrained by power, heat, and size. Moving computation to the cloud adds communication delays.

That doesn’t mean a unified model is impossible. But with current compute, a practical approach is to let a slower system handle high-level reasoning while a fast controller handles immediate actions. The challenge is getting the benefits of both within one system without compromising responsiveness.

r001.rationale: The response says current compute struggles to combine complex reasoning with low-latency control, but it does not state that a large reasoning-capable model cannot make five to ten decisions per second.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that reasoning and real-time control place very different demands on a model. For reasoning, you may want a large model that spends more time thinking through a task. But for control, the robot has to respond quickly and consistently. If it loses its balance, it cannot wait several seconds for the model to decide what to do.

So the question is not just whether we have enough compute to run a very capable model. It is whether we can run that model with sufficiently low latency, while processing sensor inputs and controlling the robot, within the power and thermal limits of the hardware on the robot.

Today, a practical approach is to separate those timescales: a higher-level model reasons about what to do, and a faster controller handles execution. A unified model would need to deliver both capabilities without sacrificing either. I don’t think that is fundamentally impossible, but current compute makes it a difficult tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response says current compute makes it difficult to run a capable model with low latency, but it does not state that the model cannot run at five to ten decisions per second.
